primary_sources: Charles Gustrine, "True Sons of Freedom" poster, 1918

stimulus.text: The poster shows Black American soldiers in uniform charging forward with rifles and bayonets under an American flag, as German soldiers surrender on the right. A portrait of Abraham Lincoln looks on from the upper right, beside the words "Liberty And Freedom Shall Not Perish" — A. Lincoln. Text on the left reads: "COLORED MEN / The First Americans / Who Planted / Our Flag / on the Firing Line." At the bottom: "TRUE SONS OF FREEDOM." The poster was drawn by Charles Gustrine in 1918.
stimulus.source_note: Poster by Charles Gustrine, 1918, public domain (Library of Congress LCCN93503146). The 'Liberty And Freedom Shall Not Perish — A. Lincoln' line is the poster's own wording, a paraphrase of the Gettysburg Address, not a documented Lincoln quotation.

source: original; stimulus image from the shared pool, Charles Gustrine poster, 1918, public domain
stem: The poster was created most directly to encourage Black men to

options.text: move to northern cities to find factory work
options.misconception: The poster shows soldiers charging into battle, not workers moving to factories.

options.text: vote for the Republican Party in 1918
options.misconception: The poster says nothing about voting or any party.

options.text: demand an end to segregation in the South
options.misconception: The poster calls Black men to serve, not to demand an end to segregation.

options.text: enlist in the army and serve in the war

rationales.A: The poster shows soldiers charging into battle, not workers moving to factories.
rationales.B: The poster says nothing about voting or any party.
rationales.C: The poster calls Black men to serve, not to demand an end to segregation.
rationales.D: The poster calls Black men "True Sons of Freedom" and shows them charging as soldiers under the flag. It is a recruiting poster.
rationales.general:
1. Look at the picture. Black soldiers charge forward with rifles under the American flag.
2. Read the words. "True Sons of Freedom" and "Colored Men" name the audience and praise their service.
3. Note the portrait. Lincoln looks on from the corner, tying this service to the freedom he proclaimed.
4. Name the ask. The poster wants Black men to enlist.
Remember: a poster's audience and its action are both written on its face.

figures.caption: Black soldiers charge under the flag as Lincoln looks on, with the words “True Sons of Freedom.”
